text: Every circuit you've run so far has gone to a local simulator you fully control. The moment you point at real IBM Quantum hardware, you're choosing between multiple physical devices with different qubit counts, layouts, queues, and native gate sets — and that choice meaningfully affects whether your circuit runs well, slowly, or at all.

qiskit-ibm-runtime is the current library for talking to real hardware. Once your credentials are saved, you create a QiskitRuntimeService and ask it for backends. least_busy with operational=True and simulator=False filters out anything offline or under maintenance, excludes cloud simulators, and returns whichever real device currently has the shortest queue — usually a better starting point than hardcoding a device name.

Four real criteria drive backend selection. Qubit count: your circuit needs at least as many physical qubits as it uses logically, but that's necessary, not sufficient. Queue length: a shorter queue on a smaller device often beats a longer line on a bigger, more popular one. Connectivity, the coupling map: which physical qubit pairs support a native two-qubit gate. And the basis gate set: the specific native gates a given backend can actually execute, which any circuit gets rewritten into regardless of what gates you wrote.

IBM retires and introduces processors, adjusts free-tier access, and rebalances queues on an ongoing basis. Treat any specific device name, qubit count, or availability claim you read anywhere, including in this course, as a snapshot that may be stale. The IBM Quantum Platform dashboard is the authoritative, current source for which backends exist and what their queues look like right now.

Next lesson follows your circuit past backend selection into the mandatory translation step that happens before anything runs: transpilation, and why the circuit that actually executes is never quite the one you wrote.
